articles.title: I closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’
articles.summary: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France. An unruly rabble bursts on to the street: a noisy eruption, bubbling towards us.
body: My partner and I had set off by Eurostar less than 24 hours before, yet this place felt a world away from the ad agency where I work.

We’d booked cheap tickets to Paris months ago, intending to plan a trip on from there by train. As our departure approached, Instagram seemed to be full of aspirational, yet similar, holiday photos, and almost every other TikTok post I flicked past offered the promise of a hidden destination … discovered.

I find ratings, reviews and recommendations just as reassuring as the next person, especially when faced with a limited holiday allowance. The safety of the search bar helps to give me the confidence that I’m spending my hard earned money as wisely as possible. I work in a world that runs on data and optimisation and I love it, but I wondered whether I’d optimised the adventure out of my own holidays.
So, we tried a simple experiment. We closed down the tabs and opened a map of western Europe. Embracing a bit of low-tech randomness, we chose to let chance decide our trip.
points: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance.
Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France.

articles.title: A moment that changed me: I was devastated by a breakup – and saved by a sweaty moshpit
articles.summary: When my relationship broke down, my usual playlist of pop girl anthems and love songs left me in tears. Then I discovered hardcore punk. Nobody warned me that heartbreak would ruin my relationship with Beyoncé.
body: When I listened to the artists I loved most, I was ambushed by memories and reminded of all the love and intimacy I had lost. My usual playlists, filled with indie bops and pop girl anthems, became unbearable. I’d never noticed before, but almost every song was about love, yearning, romance and sex. Every time I pressed play, I found myself sobbing in the shower or ugly-crying in public.

Tired of burning through tissues, I decided to go no contact with music. In fact, I was determined to avoid the topic of love at all costs. You would be surprised how much that limits what you can do, because, to paraphrase Hugh Grant in Love Actually, love is – unfortunately – all around. I swapped my playlists for journalism podcasts, true-crime audiobooks and soothing ambient noise, but nothing seemed to fill the space that the lack of music had left in my life.

“What’s the genre furthest away from my usual taste?” I wondered, scrolling through Spotify, a few months post-breakup. I clicked recklessly, ending up in a hardcore punk playlist. Not knowing where to begin, I pressed play on the first band on the list.

Nobody warned me that heartbreak would ruin my relationship with Beyoncé.

articles.title: Veggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradise
articles.summary: In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them. Sixty bowls of slime-green soup sit waiting for the children to arrive.
body: This is a typical Thursday lunchtime in BS De Stadspoort primary school in Ghent, Belgium. Similar meat-free menus are being eaten in other schools and nurseries across the city, plus community centres, care homes and assisted living facilities, not to mention many work canteens and restaurants. Thursday in Ghent is officially “Veggie Day”, with residents encouraged to eschew any meat or fish. So how did a city get its children – and everyone else – to eat their greens?

It didn’t happen overnight. “The success story of Ghent is one where we had an amazing grassroots movement, with people asking for more climate action. But the magic happened when politicians actually listened and implemented policy to introduce the Thursday Veggie Day in 2009,” says Vanessa Debruyne, the head of communications for the nonprofit organisation ProVeg Belgium, who is showing me around town. “It got the ball rolling, companies and restaurants joined, the population got used to it, and more entrepreneurs made the move to plant-based. We’ve been unstoppable ever since! Ghent is the best town in Belgium for plant-based food.”

articles.title: What It’s Like to Be a Casting Director in 2026
articles.summary: Vogue Business tracked four casting directors through the SS27 season, to understand what it really takes to scout, negotiate and book models for a runway show.
body: “When someone walks towards you, you’re going to have two reactions. You’re going to have one that’s personal to you, and you’re going to have one that is very analytical, one that’s ‘right for my client’,” says Grimes, who worked on eight other shows this Spring/Summer 2027 season, including Jil Sander, Victoria Beckham, Missoni, MM6 Maison Margiela, and Erdem. While the live casting moment feels intense, the decisions that determine who walks, and who doesn’t, are the visible end of a process that starts long before any hopeful model enters the room.

Ten years ago, brands would largely select their own models for their runways and campaigns. “Casting has [evolved] because of the volume of projects that brands feel like they need to do,” Grimes says. “You can’t just have a campaign that’s out in magazines for four months and then move on to the next. People are scrolling all day, so they need new imagery to see.” Some of luxury’s biggest players will stage five or six runway shows a year, plus near-monthly campaigns for categories, from bags to eyewear.

articles.title: Fast-fashion giant Shein outperforms several Australian retailers on ethics, report says
articles.summary: Ghanda and Windsor Smith are among lowest-rated in Baptist World Aid ethical fashion report based on metrics such as wages and sustainability. Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
body: Online fast-fashion giant Shein is outperforming many Australian high street retailers on ethical standards, according to an industry review.
The 11th Baptist World Aid ethical fashion report, released on Tuesday, assessed the ethical practices of 138 Australian and international companies, representing 543 fashion brands.
Overall, the report found that only 13% of the fashion companies surveyed could show evidence of paying a living wage to any of the workers in their supply chain.
The organisation surveys companies on five broad supply chain topics, including worker empowerment and environmental sustainability, to score brands out of 100.

articles.title: The ‘Tavern-Style’ Pizza Takeover
articles.summary: In the suburbs of Chicago where they both grew up, it was just pizza, according to Brittany and Brennan Grosvenor, the couple behind Proof in Portland, Oregon. Ordering came down to the question of “thin-crust, deep-dish, or double-dough,” Brittany recalls of her family’s Friday night tradition.
body: Outsiders might associate Chicago with its famous, tourist-beckoning deep-dish pizza, but Brittany says that’s just not reflective of reality, citing deep dish as a much less frequent treat than the Midwestern, thin-crust style that’s gaining popularity. “The pizza you get every week, or if you go to a kid’s birthday party, it’s always tavern-style,” she says.

“Tavern-style” pizza — which is prevalent across the Midwest, with Chicago, Milwaukee, Minnesota, and St. Louis touting similar pies — is known for its thin, cracker-like crust, cut into a lattice instead of triangular slices. Depending on the region and the pizza shop where one’s nostalgia lies, the sauce might lean sweet or spicy. Lightness and crispness, though, is the style’s unique sell. Writing for Esquire in 2023, Omar Mamoon called the variant, which was then still on the rise, “a foil” to famously thick Detroit-style pizza, which had its big moment in the late 2010s.

articles.title: How Luxury Is Showing Up for Diwali Across the World
articles.summary: Diwali can be a meaningful moment on luxury’s global calendar, but there’s room for more investment in regions beyond India.
body: Diwali is now firmly on luxury’s global calendar, offering brands an opportunity to connect with Indian customers while tapping into the festival’s growing commercial potential. But while brands have learned how to make Ramadan and Lunar New Year meaningful moments in their marketing calendars, Diwali is still a work in progress.

Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights, with its name originating from the Sanskrit word for “row of lights”. Its dates follow the lunar calendar, and the five-day festival begins with Dhanteras, an auspicious occasion for buying gold and jewelry, before culminating in Bhai Dooj. The main day, Lakshmi Puja, falls on November 8 this year. Celebrated by Hindus, Jains and Sikhs, not across India as a whole, Diwali encompasses different regional traditions and customs.
points: Diwali can be a meaningful moment on luxury’s global calendar, but there’s room for more investment in regions beyond India.

articles.title: Zane Li of Lii Is the Winner of the 2026 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund
articles.summary: As this year's CVFF winner, Zane Li will take home a $300,000 cash prize and industry mentorship dedicated to the further growth of his young brand.
body: Tonight at Crane Club, Zane Li, of Lii, was announced as the 2026 winner of the CFDA/ Vogue Fashion Fund. The Chongqing-born, New York-based designer has had quite the year. In April, Li took home the Fashion Trust US Ready-to-Wear Award, and in September, he was declared the winner of the Karl Lagerfeld Prize at the LVMH Prize ceremony in Paris.

At the start of the CVFF finalist process, Li spoke of the financial challenges of running a young brand. “The business side [is the difficult part],” he said. “When you start to consider the income, the revenue, the loss, and the money you spend, suddenly you’re turning your interest into a job. The most rewarding part: You get to control everything. You get to pick your show music, which is my favorite part of doing a show. You get to pick what the color of the carpet is at your show space, and you get to decide what kind of styles you want to sell.”
Li rounds out 2026 with a third cash prize, $300,000 from the CFDA/ Vogue Fashion Fund, and further mentorship from industry experts.

articles.title: In Her Sequel to 'Big Little Lies,' Liane Moriarty Shines a Light on Suburban Australia's Dark Side
articles.summary: The lifelong Sydneysider on why her home country is the only place that her novels could be set—and how it felt to see them translated to California on the silver screen.
body: “I don't actually think a sense of place is one of my strengths. I find dialogue and character come easily to me, but I'm not somebody who describes scenery particularly well, and I have a very poor memory about anywhere that I've visited. I remember the people that I meet, but I find it hard to remember the actual places, which is why I always set all my books in Australia—I can literally look out the window and see where I am!

Definitely with Big Little Lies and Big Little Truths, the lives of these characters seem amazing, but when you dig deeper there are all these threats. I'm always interested in characters who look like they've got it all together and perhaps they don't, and how real people present themselves to the world versus what's really going on. If you've ever developed a friendship, you might have an instant first impression and then as you get to know them, you realize, oh, actually, they're this sort of person. And in the same way it's interesting to have a really beautiful setting and then explore the dark things that can happen behind closed doors.
